Lists borrow their owner; tensors pin their owner and preserve strides; Series retain independent zero-copy chunk snapshots so subsequent alias replacement does not invalidate the view. Sequence descriptors cannot be returned, stored, captured by a generator, reassigned, or used to mutate the source. Materialize an owned result instead: var owned: list[i64] = list(values, max_items=1000) list(input, max_items=N) copies nonnullable numeric values once. Sized inputs may omit the bound; exceeding a supplied nonnegative bound raises ValueError without publishing a truncated list. Allocation sizes remain overflow-checked. Nullable storage is deliberately not supported in owned lists; fill/filter first. IRx single-pass generators are not sequences and require max_items . Materialization probes at most N + 1 items to detect excess, releasing partial output and owned temporary frames on failure. Consumption is not rolled back. Named iterators are borrowed from their lexical owner and remain advanced after failure. Arx source-level generator declarations are still unsupported; this iterator workflow is available to ASTx/IRx hosts, not new Arx yield syntax.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Read-only numeric consumers

text: Tensors Fixed-shape tensors use one or more integer dimensions: fn pick(grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2]) -> i32: return grid[1, 0] fn main() -> i32: var grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] return pick(grid) Rules: supported elements: signed/unsigned 8-64-bit integers, f32 , and f64 literals must be rectangular and match the declared shape indexing supplies one index per static dimension variables, fields, and returns require at least one static dimension Tensor storage is readonly in the current implementation tensor[T, ...] accepts runtime shape/stride metadata at a function or extern parameter boundary: fn accept(values: tensor[i32, ...]) -> none: return none Indexing uses runtime rank, shape, strides, and offset. All indices must be nonnegative and in bounds, including dynamic indices into static-shaped tensors. Rank mismatch and invalid metadata fail before reading; byte-offset arithmetic is overflow-checked. Rank-one tensors also support len and ordered iteration.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Tensors

text: DataFrames and Series fn main() -> i32: var rows: dataframe[id: i32, score: f64] = dataframe({ id: [1, 2, 3], score: [0.5, 0.8, 1.0], }) var scores: series[f64] = rows.score var ids: series[i32] = rows["id"] print(rows.ncols()) return cast(rows.nrows(), i32) Rules: columns support signed/unsigned numeric, Boolean and string values nullable columns use T | none ; date/time/timestamp columns can be populated through literal constructors or checked RecordBatch conversions the constructor accepts list-literal columns with equal row counts; it does not add implicit signed-to-unsigned coercion names and types must match the declared static schema statically known columns use rows.name or rows["name"] nrows() and ncols() return i64 dataframe[...] supports runtime-schema locals, parameters and returns, preserving rich Arrow types/metadata through RecordBatch casts; its columns cannot be accessed statically by name or silently narrowed Use read_csv / write_csv from stdlib.csv and read_parquet / write_parquet from stdlib.parquet for file I/O. Reads return independently owned runtime-schema frames; writes borrow frames and check finalization. No format-specific DataFrame methods or to_* aliases are added. CSVStream and ParquetStream in those modules support explicit streaming via frame() and write(frame) . Schema , BatchBuilder , RecordBatch and IPC remain in stdlib.arrow . File workflows and format-specific safety limits live in CSV and Parquet ; exact casts follow the shared conversion contract below. IPCReader.next() advances one batch; batch() and schema() return independent snapshots. open_file selects IPC file format, open_stream selects streaming format at a path, and connect exchanges IPC streaming bytes over TCP. Writers reject schema mismatches, including metadata and nullability. Check is_null before typed getters. Objects close on their last scoped reference; explicit close() is idempotent. See the interoperability workflow and ownership contract .
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · DataFrames and Series

text: Checked DataFrame conversion cast(frame, dataframe[id:i64]) and cast(batch, dataframe[id:i64]) assert exact names, order, physical types, and every chunk's reachable nullability. They do not project, coerce, fill nulls, or infer compile-time types. Metadata and independent ownership are preserved; cast(frame, RecordBatch) bridges back to batch APIs. Runtime-schema frames preserve rich Arrow data without permitting unchecked static column access. Fixed-row-count casts, owned globals, generator locals, aggregate-owned fields, and arbitrary DataFrame FFI are unsupported. See parameterized schemas for nested nullability and exact physical parameters. File-format restrictions still apply independently of what an in-memory frame can hold.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Checked DataFrame conversion

text: Runtime boundary IRx activates native Arrow features only when lowering requires them. Generated LLVM calls opaque C ABI functions; Arrow C++ object layouts and ownership do not leak into LLVM structs or Arx syntax. See Native Apache Arrow Support for arrays, Arrow C Data, RecordBatch IPC, and current interoperability details.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Runtime boundary

text: Nullable scalars and Series expressions nullable[T] stores a fixed-width numeric or Boolean scalar plus a validity bit. A nullable column is spelled series[T | none] . Indexing a nullable column returns nullable[T] ; indexing a non-nullable column returns T . Indices are zero-based; negative or out-of-range indices fail at runtime. ``` title: Nullable column expressions ``` fn main() -> i32: var frame: dataframe[x:i32 | none] = dataframe({x:[1, none, 3]}) var doubled: series[i32 | none] = frame.x + frame.x var missing: nullable[i32] = doubled[1] assert is_null(missing) assert fill_null(doubled[2], 0) == 6 var filled: series[i32] = fill_null(doubled, 7) assert filled[1] == 7 var empty: nullable[i32] = none assert is_null(empty) return 0 Supported operators are + , - , * , / , == , != , < , <= , > and >= . Numeric operands use IRx common-type promotion. Column casts are checked; values that cannot be represented by the promoted type fail explicitly. Series/scalar operations broadcast the scalar. Series/Series operations require equal lengths. Integer arithmetic is checked: overflow and division by zero fail instead of wrapping. Null operands produce null outputs, including comparisons. Boolean && / and and || / or propagate nulls strictly, not with Kleene semantics. These operations are eager, not short-circuiting. is_null returns bool for a nullable scalar or a non-nullable Boolean Series mask. fill_null(value, replacement) eagerly evaluates a matching non-null scalar replacement and returns a non-nullable scalar or Series. Nullable scalars cannot implicitly become non-nullable values or conditions. Nullable scalar globals support numeric/Boolean literal or none initializers. Direct none is accepted in nullable declarations, assignments, returns, and function arguments/defaults. It never implicitly fills a non-nullable value. These scalar operations currently cover i8 – i64 , u8 – u64 , f32 , f64 and bool . String, temporal, decimal and nested Series retain their data and schema but cannot yet be indexed into language scalars or used in these operators. Unary + and checked - support signed numeric values; Boolean ! / not invert validity-preserving masks. Unsigned negation requires an explicit cast. Word not binds below comparisons, as in not frame.x == 3 ; see the Boolean evaluation contract . Remainder % is scalar-only and is rejected for nullable values and Series. column[start:stop:step] follows Python's bound clipping and negative-stride rules; omitted bounds are allowed and a zero step fails. Slicing, is_null and series_count also work on rich column storage. series_sum , series_min , series_max , series_mean , series_any and series_all skip nulls and return nullable scalars: empty/all-null input has a null result. series_count returns the non-null count as i64 . Integer sums use checked i64 / u64 accumulators; floating sums and means return f64 . Boolean reductions require Boolean columns. column[index] = value updates a mutable numeric/Boolean Series binding with bounds, type and nullability checks. Aliases of that handle observe updates; the originating DataFrame and previously computed/sliced Series do not. Construction completes before publication, so failed updates leave the old column intact. Concurrent access to a mutated handle is unsupported. Updates are statements, not value-producing assignment expressions. Returned Series own independent references; temporary columns and aliases are released by normal scope-lifetime cleanup.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Nullable scalars and Series expressions

text: Parameterized static DataFrame schemas Checked RecordBatch casts additionally accept: decimal128[precision, scale] and decimal256[precision, scale] . timestamp["unit"] , timestamp["unit", "timezone"] , and time["unit"] , with units s , ms , us or ns . binary , binary[positive_size] , large_binary , and large_string . arrow_list[T] , large_list[T] , and fixed_list[T, positive_size] . dictionary[index_type, value_type] (unordered). arrow_map[key_type, value_type] and arrow_struct[name:T, ...] . For example, dataframe[amount:decimal128[12, 3] | none, items:arrow_list[nullable[i32]] | none] declares nullable decimal and list columns. Nested children are non-nullable unless wrapped in nullable[T] ; this wrapper models child nullability even for types that cannot be language scalars. Map keys cannot be nullable. Rich schemas work in aliases, parameters, returns and checked RecordBatch casts. Casts check names, order, exact physical parameters and nested nullability; non-nullable top-level columns also check actual batch null counts. They do not rescale decimals, change time units, or decode dictionaries implicitly. Input schema and field metadata are preserved. Unparameterized time uses time64 microseconds; timestamp / datetime use timezone-naive timestamp microseconds. Their text literal constructors accept whole seconds without timezone or fractional components. Use parameterized storage or checked Arrow imports for other units or zones. Rich DataFrame literals use the declared schema rather than inference. Decimal cells use exact strings or integers (not binary floats); binary cells use UTF-8 strings, with fixed widths checked in bytes. Parameterized temporal cells use integer storage units, without timezone conversion. Lists use nested lists; structs use positional lists matching declared field order; maps use lists of [key, value] pairs. Dictionaries encode literal values with checked index capacity. Nested nullability, widths, precision, scale and shape are validated during semantic analysis. Lowering embeds validated Arrow IPC bytes, not a Python interpreter or handwritten serialization format. Standalone rich scalar variables remain unsupported.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Parameterized static DataFrame schemas

text: Arx Compiler CLI The arxlang distribution installs the arx command. It can inspect frontend and lowering stages, compile native artifacts, run executables, and execute compiled tests. Command forms arx [input_file] [options] arx run [input_file] [options] arx test [paths ...] [options] run is an alternate spelling of --run . test is a separate subcommand. Inspection modes arx --show-tokens program.x arx --show-ast program.x arx --show-llvm-ir program.x These modes stop after printing the requested representation. Build and run arx program.x --output-file program arx --run program.x arx run program.x The compiler emits an executable when the module defines main . Without a native entry point, or with --lib , it emits an object artifact instead. Use arx --help for the complete option list and defaults rather than a copied flag catalog. Diagnostics and linker choices below have operational consequences. Compiling multiple input files in one invocation is not currently supported. Use project-aware imports to compile a module graph from one entry file. Output path --output-file accepts the requested artifact path. If it is omitted, the compiler derives a name from the entry source file and otherwise falls back to a.out . Link modes The default auto mode uses the platform toolchain's default executable mode. pie and no-pie request explicit position-independent or non-PIE linking. If a linker defaults to PIE but rejects an object relocation, use: arx program.x --link-mode no-pie IRx emits PIC-compatible objects by default. Explicit link modes are primarily toolchain compatibility controls. Diagnostics Expected lexer, parser, semantic, lowering, native compilation, and linking failures exit with status 1. Human-readable diagnostics go to standard error by default. Unexpected internal failures produce ARX-INTERNAL-001 without exposing exception details and exit with status 70. Compiler developers can opt in to the original Python exception and traceback with --traceback . Use --diagnostic-format json for one versioned JSON document on standard error: { "diagnostics": [ { "code": "ARX-PARSE-001", "column": 7, "end_column": null, "end_line": null, "hint": null, "line": 4, "message": "expected expression", "module": null, "notes": [], "phase": "frontend", "severity": "error" } ], "schema_version": 1 } JSON mode covers expected compiler-phase failures and sanitized internal failures. Argument usage errors remain argparse text with exit status 2. Consumers must reject unsupported schema_version values instead of guessing field semantics. Exit status Meaning 0 command succeeded 1 expected compiler/source failure 2 CLI usage or input-path failure 70 unexpected internal compiler failure Tests The arx test subcommand has its own discovery and execution options. See Compiled Tests . API boundary CLI argument handling lives in Arx. Semantic diagnostics, LLVM lowering, artifact building, and runtime feature activation are provided by IRx.

text: Control Flow Arx supports if / elif / else , while , and two for loop styles. If / Elif / Else Conditions must be Boolean and are evaluated in order, stopping at the first match. A chain may have any number of elif clauses and an optional final else . Align every clause with its opening if ; use elif , not else if . ``` title: Conditional chain example summary: Classifies an integer using ordered comparisons. ``` fn classify(value: i32) -> i32: ``` title: classify summary: Classifies one integer as negative, zero, or positive. ``` if value < 0: return 0 - 1 elif value == 0: return 0 else: return 1 While Loop ``` title: While loop example summary: Repeats while condition is true. ``` fn count_to_ten() -> i32: ``` title: count_to_ten summary: Increments value until it reaches ten. ``` var a: i32 = 0 while a < 10: a = a + 1 return a For Loop (For-In Style) For-in loops iterate over list-valued expressions, including builtin range(start, stop[, step]) , list literals, and list variables: for i in <list-expression>: ``` title: Range-style for loop summary: Iterates from start to end with the builtin range helper. ``` fn range_loop(n: i32) -> i32: ``` title: range_loop summary: Sums values produced by a range loop. ``` var total: i32 = 0 for i in range(0, n): total = total + i return total You can also iterate over a list literal or a list variable: ``` title: List for-in loop summary: Iterates over one list variable and one list literal. ``` fn list_loop() -> i32: ``` title: list_loop summary: Sums values from two list-valued loop inputs. ``` var values: list[i32] = range(0, 3) var total: i32 = 0 for value in values: total = total + value for value in [3, 4]: total = total + value return total The old colon range header syntax was removed. Use builtin range(...) or any other list-valued expression instead. For Loop (Count Style) Count-style loops follow: for var i: type = init; condition; update: ``` title: Count-style for loop summary: Uses initializer, condition, and update expressions. ``` fn count_loop() -> i32: ``` title: count_loop summary: Sums numbers from 0 to 4. ``` var total: i32 = 0 for var i: i32 = 0; i < 5; i += 1: total += i return total Compound updates write the induction variable themselves. Ordinary expression updates such as i + 1 remain supported; the loop stores their result into i . See the compound assignment contract . Return Statements return expr returns a value from the current function. Inside none -returning functions, use a bare return , return none , or omit the return statement entirely. Indentation Rules Blocks start after : . The next logical line must be indented by one level (2 spaces in Arx style). Misaligned indentation is treated as a parser error.

text: CSV files and DataFrames Import CSV operations from stdlib.csv . Shared Arrow schemas, batches and IPC remain in stdlib.arrow ; CSV is backed by Arrow C++, not a Python process or a second parser. The native Arrow libraries and a C++ toolchain are required. Read and write a DataFrame ``` title: Copy a CSV file ``` import (read_csv, write_csv) from stdlib.csv fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Read every row and finalize the output ``` var frame: dataframe[...] = read_csv("input.csv") write_csv(frame, "output.csv") return 0 These eager functions close their internal session before returning. Reads return an independent, chunked DataFrame; writes borrow the frame without consuming or mutating it. Temporary inputs such as write_csv(read_csv("input.csv"), "output.csv") are supported. The result must fit in memory: block_size controls parsing blocks, not total memory. Writers return none only after checked finalization. There are no DataFrame .to_* methods or to_* aliases. Never copy a file onto itself using streaming sessions. Parsing policy An omitted schema is inferred from the first block, then frozen. For headerless input, supply a schema or explicit names; names requires header=false and no schema. Projections must be nonempty and unique and preserve requested order. null_values replaces token recognition; an empty list disables it. These choices affect interpretation, not just performance. The eager option schema lives in irx.analysis.table_io ; defaults and validation are implemented by the native CSV options code. Python signatures are in the generated table_io reference. Stream declarations and contracts live in packages/arx/src/arx/stdlib/csv.x . Arx name/column/token arguments are literal lists, not arbitrary iterable objects. Unknown options and unsupported types fail explicitly. Delimiter, quote and escape bytes must not conflict; NUL, CR and LF are not valid dialect characters. Output quoting uses Arrow's fixed double-quote convention; this is not a complete Python csv dialect engine. CSV projection happens after full input validation and conversion . A bad unselected field still fails. Explicit schemas check header names/order/count and nullability; they control parsing rather than merely asserting types. Checked DataFrame conversion import Schema from stdlib.arrow import read_csv from stdlib.csv # Inside a function: var schema: Schema = Schema() schema.add("id", "int64", nullable=false) var loaded: dataframe[...] = read_csv("ids.csv", schema=schema) var ids: dataframe[id:i64] = cast(loaded, dataframe[id:i64]) Runtime schemas do not infer compile-time column types. The cast above asserts an exact schema; it does not project or coerce data. See the shared checked DataFrame conversion contract for nullability, chunk validation, metadata, and ownership restrictions. CSV supports integer widths, floating point, Boolean, UTF-8/large UTF-8, dates, timestamps and time units. Nested/other unsupported types fail; use Parquet or IPC for those. CSV does not encode type/schema metadata. Supply an explicit schema to preserve widths and temporal units on a roundtrip. Explicit streaming Use CSVStream for incremental processing instead of loading the entire file into a DataFrame. It supports either read or write mode. import CSVStream from stdlib.csv # Inside a function: var source: CSVStream = CSVStream() source.open_read("large.csv") while source.next(): var chunk: dataframe[...] = source.frame() print(chunk.nrows()) source.close() CSVStream() starts closed and has one read or write mode. open_read_as(path, schema, ...) supplies an explicit schema; open_write(path, schema, ...) configures output. These session factories expose delimiter/header and read block size. The additional dialect controls above belong to the eager functions. next() advances; false means EOF, not an empty batch. frame() snapshots the current batch without advancing and survives reader closure. It fails before a successful next() or after EOF. write(frame) and write(batch) require an exact schema. batch() and schema() remain available for Arrow interoperability. Call writer close() explicitly to observe finalization errors; automatic cleanup alone is not proof of success. Wrong-mode access fails, aliases share session state, and failed sessions cannot be reused. The streaming roundtrip example processes every batch. The table example converts CSV to Parquet using only the module-level functions. Text and failure contract UTF-8 and quoted multiline fields are supported. By default only unquoted empty fields are null. Quoted "" remains an empty string; NA and NULL remain text unless configured in null_values . Custom na_rep requires matching read null_values . Non-null unquoted data equal to a null marker is ambiguous; a lossless roundtrip is not guaranteed. Blank one-column rows remain null rows unless explicitly skipped. Malformed record widths fail; skiprows does not enable malformed-row skipping. Headers must be nonempty and unique. Typed header-only input succeeds; completely empty files fail. Inferred null/binary columns need an explicit supported schema or corrected input. CSV has no remote URLs, compression/encoding discovery, append or atomic writes. Validation precedes truncation, but later data/I/O failures can leave partial output. A failed eager read never returns a partial table. Compiled failures use ARX-RUNTIME-ARROW-001 , with typed catchable Arx exceptions. CSV row positions are not invented as Arx source locations. Python integration from irx.table_io import read_csv, write_csv frame = read_csv("input.tsv", delimiter="\t", columns=["id", "name"]) write_csv(frame, "output.csv") These functions return/accept pyarrow.Table , accept string or PathLike paths, and use IRx native sessions/C Stream interchange, not Python format engines. Use pyarrow.Schema for schema . Selectors accept checked sequences. Imports do not compile native code; CSV-only use does not load Parquet, Dataset or Acero. Stale native-library overrides produce a rebuild/unset error. For streaming, irx.record_batch.CSVStream and the lower-level RecordBatchStreamReader.open_csv / RecordBatchStreamWriter.open_csv remain available. Iteration releases its batch on advancement; batch.to_arrow() exports independent Arrow references. Release manually retained batch/schema snapshots explicitly.

The table example converts CSV to Parquet using only the module-level functions.

text: Text and failure contract UTF-8 and quoted multiline fields are supported. By default only unquoted empty fields are null. Quoted "" remains an empty string; NA and NULL remain text unless configured in null_values . Custom na_rep requires matching read null_values . Non-null unquoted data equal to a null marker is ambiguous; a lossless roundtrip is not guaranteed. Blank one-column rows remain null rows unless explicitly skipped. Malformed record widths fail; skiprows does not enable malformed-row skipping. Headers must be nonempty and unique. Typed header-only input succeeds; completely empty files fail. Inferred null/binary columns need an explicit supported schema or corrected input. CSV has no remote URLs, compression/encoding discovery, append or atomic writes. Validation precedes truncation, but later data/I/O failures can leave partial output. A failed eager read never returns a partial table. Compiled failures use ARX-RUNTIME-ARROW-001 , with typed catchable Arx exceptions. CSV row positions are not invented as Arx source locations.
title: CSV files and DataFrames · Text and failure contract

text: Python integration from irx.table_io import read_csv, write_csv frame = read_csv("input.tsv", delimiter="\t", columns=["id", "name"]) write_csv(frame, "output.csv") These functions return/accept pyarrow.Table , accept string or PathLike paths, and use IRx native sessions/C Stream interchange, not Python format engines. Use pyarrow.Schema for schema . Selectors accept checked sequences. Imports do not compile native code; CSV-only use does not load Parquet, Dataset or Acero. Stale native-library overrides produce a rebuild/unset error. For streaming, irx.record_batch.CSVStream and the lower-level RecordBatchStreamReader.open_csv / RecordBatchStreamWriter.open_csv remain available. Iteration releases its batch on advancement; batch.to_arrow() exports independent Arrow references. Release manually retained batch/schema snapshots explicitly.

text: Data Types Arx uses explicit type annotations for variables, function parameters, and function return types. Type Annotations Function parameters must always be typed. Function return type is declared with -> type and is always required, including -> none . Variable declarations must include an explicit type with var name: type . ``` title: Typed function signature summary: Demonstrates required parameter annotations. ``` fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32: ``` title: add summary: Returns a + b. ``` return a + b Collection annotations Runtime-shaped tensor[T, ...] remains parameter-only; indexed access requires a fixed shape. Runtime-schema dataframe[...] supports locals, aliases, parameters, and returns, but not unchecked named-column access. These are different restrictions. See collections for storage, construction, exact schema casts, and nullable operations. Type Aliases And Union Types Type aliases are top-level declarations. The type word is contextual, so type Name = ... declares an alias while type(value) calls the builtin type-name helper. ``` title: Type alias example summary: Demonstrates a finite numeric union alias. ``` type Number = i32 | i64 fn identity(value: Number) -> Number: ``` title: identity summary: Returns a numeric union value. ``` return value Union annotations use | . Numeric unions currently lower through a shared lossless numeric storage type; incompatible runtime unions are rejected. Generic union bounds constrain template membership without allocating union storage. Runtime tagged unions and runtime narrowing are not part of the current model. Choosing a type See Built-in Types for scalar choices and conversion boundaries. The lexical manifest owns accepted spellings; it is not an API support promise. Class References Declared class names denote identity-preserving, reference-managed object pointers. Local copies and owned returns keep objects alive; final release runs __del__ and drops owned fields. Acyclic instance class/string/file fields are supported, but class values in containers/unions/structs, globals/statics, and generators are rejected. See Classes for construction and lifetime rules; there is no general external ownership ABI.

text: Docstrings Arx docstrings use the Douki YAML format and are validated against the official Douki schema . Docstrings are delimited by triple backticks: ``` title: Example docstring summary: Optional summary value. ``` Supported Targets (Current) module docstring class docstring function docstring method docstring Required Field Every docstring must provide at least: title (required by Douki schema) Valid minimal docstring: ``` title: Add two numbers ``` Module Docstring Rule The module docstring must: be the first top-level statement start at line 1, column 1 (no leading spaces) Valid: ``` title: Module docs ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Entry point for the module. ``` return 1 Function Docstring Rule A function docstring, when present, must be the first statement in the function body, right after : and the required newline/indentation. The parser does not require a docstring in every user function; repository source-contract conventions still apply. Valid: fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Function docs summary: Function summary ``` return 1 Invalid: fn main() -> i32: return 1 ``` title: Too late summary: This docstring is valid Douki but in the wrong position. ``` Class and method docstrings A class docstring may appear as the first item in an indented class body, before fields or methods. text: File I/O File is a builtin reference-managed class for a deliberately small native, POSIX text and binary file interface. open(...) is a compiler-backed factory adapter to File(...) : both create the same class object through one checked construction path. Both are available without an import and use C stdio, not Python or Arrow. Lowercase file remains a compatibility spelling for the builtin File type. The default is a strict UTF-8 text read. Use mode="w" to create/truncate or mode="a" to append. Only the path and mode can be runtime strings; other Python-shaped settings accept only the implemented default profile. Nondefault buffering, encodings, error policies, newline handling, descriptors, and openers are rejected rather than ignored. Options are checked before I/O; a dynamic mode is checked before opening or truncating a path. Paths are relative to the running program's working directory, not its source file. Reading requires an existing file. Writing creates or truncates it. Appending creates it if necessary and writes at the end. Update/exclusive modes, file descriptors, callbacks, and custom buffering are unsupported. Binary modes are rb , wb , and ab ; non- none encoding, errors, or newline options are rejected before creating/truncating a path, including when the mode is dynamic. Example Run this in a scratch directory: the example creates/truncates message.txt . ``` title: Native text file example ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main ``` var output: File = File("message.txt", mode="w", encoding="utf-8") var alias: file = output assert alias.write("hello\n") == 6 output.close() alias.close() var source: file = open(file="message.txt") var text: str = source.read() source.close() print(text) return 0 Bounded binary workflow Use bytes([0, 255, 13, 10]) for octets, then output.write_bytes(data) on a binary stream. source.read_bytes(size) reads at most a nonnegative i64 byte count; there is no read-all sentinel. It returns independently owned bytes , including empty at EOF. Zero does not advance but still checks mode and closed state. Text methods reject binary streams and byte methods reject text streams. Nothing decodes, strips NUL, or translates newlines. examples/binary-files.x is an executable round-trip and append example. It creates/truncates binary-output.dat and binary-empty.dat ; run it in a scratch directory. Byte lengths and write counts are bytes, not characters. Short writes that make progress are retried; no progress and I/O errors are failures. Failure may leave a partially modified external file: there is no rollback, atomicity, or durability promise. Explicit flush/close still matter for buffered errors. See byte values for immutable-buffer ownership. Text and lifetime safety Reads consume all remaining text (not a size-limited chunk), returning an independent string or "" at EOF. CRLF and CR become LF; malformed UTF-8 and embedded NUL fail. Write counts are Unicode characters, not bytes. Explicit flush checks buffered writes without promising durability. Close is idempotent; other operations on a closed file fail. Method signatures and concise contracts live in packages/arx/src/arx/builtins/files.x . Public File values follow ordinary acyclic class-reference ownership. Aliases share one stream and cursor; closing through one reference closes it for all references. References can be reassigned, passed to functions, returned, and stored in class fields. Locals and discarded temporaries release their references on ordinary lexical exits. The last reference releases the native wrapper once, even if the stream was explicitly closed earlier. Read strings and byte buffers own independent memory and can outlive the file. See Classes . Explicit casts to or from builtin File , including identity casts, remain unsupported. Use ordinary assignment to create an alias instead. Construction opens immediately: there is no public unopened constructor, instance open() method, reopening, or builtin subclassing. A default-empty File reference is not an unopened stream; dereferencing it raises the checked class-reference error. Class containers/unions/struct fields, owned globals and statics, generator capture, and external object ownership remain unsupported. The class's native handle is private and uniquely owned. It cannot be extracted, copied, returned, or replaced by user code; NativeFileHandle is not a public Arx type. General class finalization owns its release, not a second manual handle-freeing destructor. Direct creation and I/O failures use ARX-RUNTIME-FILE-001 and raise typed exceptions (including OSError for operating-system failures). Class checks use ARX-RUNTIME-CLASS-001 ; allocation failure remains unrecoverable. Failed creation preserves constructor rollback and completed-base cleanup. See the exception boundary . Explicit close/flush are recommended to observe write errors before later work. with , iteration, seek/tell, and extra file properties are deferred. For explicit imports, use import File as TextFile from builtins.files or import builtins.files as io followed by io.File(...) . These resolve the same canonical class, not an unrelated class with the same name. Existing user or imported File / open bindings retain normal resolution; non-callable local shadowing is an error. The lowercase file type always denotes the builtin. This is a Python-like subset: parameter names/order/default spellings follow Python's interface , but UTF-8 replaces locale-dependent encoding, and NUL-containing text and many optional settings are intentionally unsupported. Existing user/imported functions named open retain normal positional-call resolution. A local non-callable open shadows the builtin and produces an error when called.
title: File I/O

text: Functions Functions are defined with fn , a name, parameters in () , and a body after : with indentation. Definition Syntax ``` title: Function definition summary: Shows the structure of a function declaration. ``` fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32: ``` title: add summary: Returns x plus y. ``` return x + y Calling Functions ``` title: Function call example summary: Defines a helper function and calls it from main. ``` fn double(v: i32) -> i32: ``` title: double summary: Returns v multiplied by two. ``` return v * 2 fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Calls double with a constant input. ``` return double(10) Keyword Arguments Ordinary functions and instance/static methods accept named arguments, including through imported aliases and module namespaces: add(y=2, x=1) add(1, y=2) helpers.add(x=1, y=2) counter.read(offset=3) identity<i32>(value=7) Positional arguments must precede keywords. Names are case-sensitive and must match the resolved declaration. Existing ordinary function-call lookup remains module-visible and separate from lexical local-value lookup; builtin/class shadowing rules are unchanged. Duplicate names, positional/name collisions, unknown names, and missing required parameters are compilation errors. A named call may end with a trailing comma. Unpacking ( *args , **kwargs ) and keyword-only/positional-only parameter declarations are not supported. The receiver is evaluated first, then all explicitly supplied values exactly once in source order, even when their names reverse parameter order. Omitted defaults run afterward in parameter declaration order. Unlike Python, Arx already evaluates defaults at call time ; they may reference earlier bound parameters, and method defaults may read self . For f(a, b=a+1, c=b+1) , f(c=9, a=2) calls with (2, 3, 9) and does not evaluate c 's default. Dynamic methods bind names/defaults through the statically selected interface, then dispatch positional values to the override. Fixed extern parameter names can be used; any existing C variadic tail stays positional and uses existing promotions. Keywords do not enable unsupported FFI types. Parser intrinsics and collection operations without a named-call schema still reject keywords. Signature-backed bundled functions such as range(start=0, stop=3) use their declared parameters, not Python overloads. Default Parameter Values Function, method, and extern parameters can declare trailing default values with = . Calls may omit defaulted parameters, including a middle default when a later parameter is supplied by name. ``` title: Default argument example summary: Calls a helper using an optional offset. ``` fn add_offset(value: i32, offset: i32 = 1) -> i32: ``` title: add_offset summary: Adds an optional offset to value. ``` return value + offset fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Uses the declared default offset. ``` return add_offset(4) Template Functions Function templates use an @<...> block on the line immediately before fn . Each template parameter must declare a bound, and bounds may be a single type or a | union of concrete types. Module-local type aliases can name and compose these bounds; importing aliases from another module is not supported. Explicit template arguments are written between the callee name and ( . ``` title: Template function example summary: Uses one bounded template parameter with inferred and explicit calls. ``` type SignedInteger = i8 | i16 | i32 | i64 type Float = f32 | f64 type Real = SignedInteger | Float @<T: Real> fn add(x: T, y: T) -> T: ``` title: add summary: Adds two values that share one template-bound type. ``` return x + y fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Calls template specializations through inference and explicit args. ``` print(add(1, 2)) assert add<f64>(1.5, 2.5) == 4.0 return 0 Here T is one concrete type, not a union-valued argument. Inferred arguments for the same T must agree in type; use explicit specialization or casts to choose conversions. Each concrete member of a bound must support the function body, so define only the numeric group that the operation actually supports. Function Body Rules The block starts after : . The next line must be indented. A function docstring (if present) must be the first element in the function block. Function docstrings must use Douki YAML and include at least title . Example: ``` title: Function docstring placement summary: Function docstring appears as the first body element. ``` fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32: ``` title: Add two numbers summary: Returns x + y. ``` return x + y Extern Prototypes Arx also supports external function declarations: Native package metadata can supply build/link requirements for resolved extern declarations. Calls retain normal parameter/keyword binding; the compiler does not infer a native dependency from a function's name. ``` title: Extern prototype example summary: Declares an external function signature. ``` extern putchard(x: i32) -> i32 Native file construction File and open share checked construction and return ordinary File references. Their restricted native settings are not arbitrary Python keyword forwarding. Class constructors bind keywords through __init__ ; ordinary function/method binding follows the rules above.

text: Getting Started with Arx This guide installs the Arx compiler and compiles a small program. See the compiler CLI for inspection and output modes. Requirements Python 3.10 or newer pip for a published installation, or Mamba/Conda and Poetry for a source checkout LLVM/Clang-compatible tools for object and executable generation a C++ compiler when a program activates native Apache Arrow features Token, ASTx, and most LLVM translation workflows do not invoke the system linker. Building or running an executable does. Install from PyPI pip install arxlang arx --version The arxlang distribution installs the arx Python package and the arx command. Its IRx dependency provides the analysis, LLVM, and native runtime layers. Install a development checkout git clone https://github.com/arxlang/arx.git cd arx mamba env create --file conda/dev.yaml conda activate arx poetry install The repository is a monorepo containing Arx, ASTx, IRx, ArxPy, ArxJIT, and the low-profile AIX experiment. Compile a program Create hello.x : ``` title: Hello module summary: Compiles a small typed Arx program. ``` fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32: ``` title: add summary: Adds two values. ``` return a + b fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Prints one result and returns success. ``` print(add(20, 22)) return 0 Inspect the compiler stages: arx --show-tokens hello.x arx --show-ast hello.x arx --show-llvm-ir hello.x Build and run: arx hello.x --output-file hello ./hello # Equivalent one-step forms arx --run hello.x arx run hello.x An executable normally defines main() -> i32 and returns 0 on success. A single main(n: i32) parameter follows the native C main ABI and receives argc . Compile an Arrow-backed value Arx tensors, DataFrames, and Series activate IRx's native Apache Arrow C++ runtime: ``` title: Arrow-backed collections summary: Uses a Tensor, DataFrame, and Series. ``` fn main() -> i32: var grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] var rows: dataframe[id: i32, score: f64] = dataframe({ id: [1, 2, 3], score: [0.5, 0.8, 1.0], }) var scores: series[f64] = rows.score assert grid[1, 0] == 3 assert rows.nrows() == 3 assert scores[2] == 1.0 return 0 The corresponding native runtime sources and linker inputs are included only when the compilation unit uses those features. Exchange Arrow data with Python stdlib.arrow adds runtime-schema RecordBatches, IPC file/stream readers and writers, and TCP clients. No new language syntax or Python serialization is needed in the Arx producer. C++20 and the installed Arrow libraries are required at build/link time. text: Arx Programming Language Independent libraries can use native package dependencies to link C ABI backends without adding domain-specific runtime features to Arx. Arx is the programming language and source frontend in the ArxLang ecosystem. The arxlang distribution provides the arx Python package and the arx command-line compiler. text: Modules A module in Arx is a source file (for example, math.x ) containing top-level statements such as imports, function definitions, and extern declarations. Module Layout ``` title: Math module example summary: Module with one documented function. ``` fn average(x: f32, y: f32) -> f32: ``` title: average summary: Returns the arithmetic mean of x and y. ``` return (x + y) * 0.5 Package Layout When a project uses the default src/ source root, or declares [build].src_dir , Arx treats files under that source root as package modules addressed by dotted names. Example project layout: . ├── .arxproject.toml ├── src │ └── geometry │ ├── __init__.x │ ├── shared │ │ └── math.x │ └── shapes │ ├── area.x │ └── helpers.x └── tests └── test_area.x With the default src/ source root: src/geometry/__init__.x is module geometry src/geometry/shared/math.x is module geometry.shared.math src/geometry/shapes/area.x is module geometry.shapes.area src/geometry/shapes/helpers.x is module geometry.shapes.helpers Use __init__.x as the package root, following the same layout idea as Python packages. Import Syntax import geometry.shapes.area import geometry.shapes.area as area import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area import circle_area as area_of_circle from geometry.shapes.area import (circle_area, square_area) from geometry.shapes.area import radius_to_diameter from .helpers import (circle_area, square_area) from .area import clamp from ..shared.math Rules: Import statements are module-level statements. Grouped imports use parentheses. Grouped imports require from . Trailing commas are allowed in grouped imports. Empty grouped imports are invalid. Absolute module paths use dotted notation. Relative imports are supported only with from imports. Relative imports use one or more leading dots before the module path. Plain relative module imports such as import .area are not supported yet. Prefer from imports when you want callable declarations without a module qualifier. Absolute Imports Use absolute dotted paths for public imports across package boundaries: import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area Installed Package Imports Arx can also resolve absolute imports from installed Arx source packages declared in [project].dependencies in .arxproject.toml . For example, if the current project declares an installed dependency that exposes a package root named local_lib , this import resolves from that installed package when no local project source shadows it: import sum2 from local_lib.stats Installed package lookup is scoped to the current Python environment running arx . The compiler reads installed distribution metadata, follows transitive dependency metadata, and uses packaged .arxproject.toml files to find Arx source roots. It does not install packages, access the network, or change generated IR/codegen behavior. For installed packages with the normal project layout, place .arxproject.toml at the packaged project root and declare both [build].src_dir and [build].package : site-packages/local_lib_project/ ├── .arxproject.toml └── src └── local_lib ├── __init__.x └── stats.x [build] src_dir = "src" package = "local_lib" With that layout, local_lib.stats resolves to site-packages/local_lib_project/src/local_lib/stats.x . Flat package layouts are also supported for packages that place .arxproject.toml and .x files directly in the package directory: site-packages/local_lib/ ├── .arxproject.toml ├── __init__.x └── stats.x Resolution precedence is: local/current project source files installed Arx dependency packages unresolved import error The reserved stdlib and internal builtins namespaces always remain owned by the compiler and cannot be replaced by installed packages. Bundled stdlib Arx ships a first-party standard library namespace called stdlib . stdlib is bundled inside the installed arx Python package stdlib modules are written in Arx; stdlib.arrow also binds the registered IRx RecordBatch native runtime stdlib modules are resolved from the installed package location, not from the user project directory local user modules are not allowed to shadow the reserved stdlib namespace Example: import math from stdlib fn main() -> i32: return math.square(4) + math.clamp(0 - 3, 0, 2) Bundled builtins Compiler-provided builtins live in bundled .x package resources, separately from the importable stdlib . They are not copied into user projects, and local sources cannot replace the reserved namespace. Ambient names are injected only when not shadowed by a declaration or import. Explicit builtins.files imports resolve the canonical File class , not a second implementation. Builtin range currently allocates a scalar list; its declaration lives in packages/arx/src/arx/builtins/generators.x . See for-in workflows and list ownership . The module name does not imply Arx supports general generators or yield . Namespace Imports Use a module alias when you want to keep names grouped under a module namespace: ``` title: Geometry namespace import summary: Call one module member through a namespace alias. ``` import geometry.shapes.area as area fn main() -> f64: ``` title: main summary: Demonstrates namespace member access. ``` return area.circle_area(10.0) Direct symbol imports remain available when you prefer shorter local names: import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area Relative Imports Use relative from imports for package-internal references. For example, inside geometry.shapes.area : import radius_to_diameter from .helpers import clamp from ..shared.math Module Docstring Arx supports module docstrings in Douki YAML format, delimited by triple backticks: ``` title: Module documentation summary: Optional summary text ``` Current placement rule: The module docstring must be the first top-level element in the file. It must begin at character 0 of line 1 (no leading spaces). Valid: ``` title: Module docs ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Entry point for the module. ``` return 1 Invalid (leading indentation before module docstring): ``` title: Module docs ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Entry point for the module. ``` return 1 For now, module docstrings are parsed and validated but ignored by AST/IR generation. stdlib.arrow exports Schema , BatchBuilder , RecordBatch , IPCReader and IPCWriter . It uses ordinary classes and nominal opaque native handles, not new keywords. See the Arrow API and examples . Native bindings are supplied only for the bundled reserved module; a user module cannot gain these bindings merely by declaring matching handle type names. Tabular standard-library modules stdlib.csv : read_csv , write_csv , and the unified streaming CSVStream owner. stdlib.parquet : read_parquet , write_parquet , ParquetStream , ParquetOptions , ParquetFilter , and where . stdlib.arrow : canonical shared Schema , RecordBatch , BatchBuilder , IPC and Arrow interoperability. Format classes are not exported from stdlib.arrow . Import shared types from that canonical module rather than through a format module. Namespace-qualified calls and explicit aliases work normally. Format functions are not global builtins, and equally named user functions receive no native privileges. CSV/shared Arrow do not activate the optional Parquet feature.

text: External Native Packages Arx libraries can ship C ABI wrappers alongside their .x sources. The compiler discovers them through normal project dependencies and links declared native features from the reachable module graph. No Python plugins or shell build hooks run during discovery. Source-only manifests are unchanged. For example, an external rendering backend can receive numeric coordinates, UTF-8 labels, and a filename and write JPEG itself. This adds no chart API or JPEG codec to Arx and does not require binary Arx File support. Manifest and distribution [project] name = "demo-native" version = "0.1.0" [build] package = "demo_native" src_dir = "src" [native] version = 1 [native.features.backend] libraries = ["m"] [[native.features.backend.artifacts]] kind = "c_source" path = "native/shim.c" include_dirs = ["native/include"] [native.modules."demo_native.bridge"] features = ["backend"] This layout contains .arxproject.toml , src/demo_native/__init__.x , src/demo_native/bridge.x , native/shim.c , and native/include/ . Include all resources in the wheel/sdist, preserving manifest-relative paths. Consumers declare the distribution in project.dependencies , install it externally, then import its modules normally. Local development uses the same contract. Version 1 supports c_source , cxx_source , object , and static_library . Source compilation requires the appropriate toolchain; objects/archives must match the target ABI. Optional system library names become individual -l arguments. The compiler never installs missing headers/libraries or downloads dependencies. Arbitrary shell hooks and compiler flags are not accepted. Absolute/traversing paths, escaping symlinks, missing inputs, unknown fields, unsupported versions/features, and invalid library names are errors. Modules must belong to the package's actual origin. Local shadow modules cannot inherit installed native capabilities, and features cannot override builtins. Mappings apply to actual top-level extern declarations, not ordinary functions or callee spellings. C symbols must match the extern names; use unique prefixes. Incompatible ABI/native requirements are rejected across modules. Reachable extern declarations may activate features even if never called; this is not call-site dead-code elimination. Unrelated installed packages add no inputs. C ABI and ownership The first route uses existing scalar/string extern support. For example, an external module might declare the following functions, implemented by its shim: ``` title: Example external native bridge ``` extern demo_create(size: i32) -> i64 extern demo_write(token: i64, filename: str) -> i32 extern demo_release(token: i64) -> i32 Use positive checked table tokens, with 0 indicating creation failure—not pointers cast to integers. The external wrapper validates stale/forged tokens and owns native allocations. A normal Arx class can keep a token in a private scalar field and release it through __del__ . Integer tokens themselves have no static resource ownership or nominal type safety; class aliases retain their ordinary shared identity and lexical cleanup. Strings borrow NUL-terminated UTF-8 storage during the call. Copy retained text. Embedded NUL is unsupported; known NUL-containing literal arguments are rejected. Owned extern string returns still require an ownership ABI and remain rejected. Return statuses and read output slots only after success. Translate native exceptions/nonlocal jumps inside the wrapper, never across Arx frames. Image dimensions, overflow, quality, and domain validation belong to the external backend. No arbitrary fatal-error unwind is added. Compiler.check , LLVM/object output, and executable compilation carry the same capabilities in isolated registries. Object output may contain unresolved externs; it is not a self-contained native distribution format. Direct pointer APIs, callbacks, dynamic loading, and general foreign-object ownership are not introduced by this metadata feature. Native compilation is a trusted build operation, not a sandbox for malicious dependencies. Compiler fixtures verify exact delivery of an existing JPEG and arbitrary binary bytes; real rendering/encoding and image correctness must be implemented and tested in the external library.

text: Parquet files and DataFrames Import operations from stdlib.parquet , independently of CSV. Shared Schema / RecordBatch and IPC remain in stdlib.arrow . All file operations use the native Arrow/Parquet engine; compiled programs do not start Python. Read and write a DataFrame ``` title: Filter and copy Parquet rows ``` import (read_parquet, write_parquet, where) from stdlib.parquet fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Filter exact rows and finalize the destination ``` var frame: dataframe[...] = read_parquet("events.parquet", columns=["name"], filters=where("id", ">", 10)) write_parquet(frame, "selected.parquet", compression="zstd", atomic=true) return 0 Reads eagerly return an independently owned, chunked DataFrame and close the reader. Writes borrow their input and return none only after checked finalization. The full result must fit in memory; batch_size is not a total memory limit. No RecordBatch conversion or DataFrame .to_* method is required. Writes are non-atomic by default and do not append unless requested. Choose atomic publication explicitly when existing output must survive a failed write; see the safe-write contract for its limits. Option declarations and validation live in irx.analysis.table_io , irx.parquet_options , and packages/arx/src/arx/stdlib/parquet.x . The generated table_io reference supplies Python signatures; the workflow and safety rules below apply to the native engine. Explicit keywords override an options snapshot even when equal to a default . Selections and filters replace, not append to, the corresponding settings. The options owner is never mutated. Unknown parameters, empty selections and unsupported values fail rather than falling back. Without options , reads inspect the path, treating files as files and directories as Hive-aware datasets; suffixes are irrelevant. Writes with partition_columns select Hive dataset mode. Explicit options preserves its existing dataset/Hive policy instead of enabling discovery automatically. Typed predicates and configuration import (ParquetFilter, ParquetOptions, where) from stdlib.parquet # Inside a function; minimum_id may be a runtime signed integer: var predicate: ParquetFilter = where("id", ">=", minimum_id) var both: ParquetFilter = predicate.and_where("active", "==", true) var options: ParquetOptions = ParquetOptions(atomic=true, durable=true) Comparisons are == , != , < , <= , > , >= , with string, signed integer, floating or Boolean values. where("name", "is_null") and is_valid omit the value. and_where returns a separate group, preserving the original. Filter columns need not be projected; nulls are excluded by ordinary comparisons. Pruning is only an optimization, never a substitute for filtering rows. OR/IN, serialized type tags and tuple-filter expressions are not this public API. Explicit streaming and ownership Use ParquetStream for incremental reading or writing. It starts closed and has one active mode. Reads advance with next() ; false means EOF, not an empty batch, and leaves the reader open. Current batch/frame snapshots require a successful advance and survive reader closure. Schema snapshots are independent, even before the first batch or after EOF. Writers require an exact input schema, including metadata and nullability. Schema snapshots describe that input; explicit normalization may change the physical schema on disk. Unsupported backends fail, never fall back to a local filename. Live cloud-provider integration is not covered by local tests. Coordination is by canonical path, not hardlink identity, and does not exclude non-IRx writers. durable=true requires atomic replacement or file rewrite append. text: Read and write a DataFrame ``` title: Filter and copy Parquet rows ``` import (read_parquet, write_parquet, where) from stdlib.parquet fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Filter exact rows and finalize the destination ``` var frame: dataframe[...] = read_parquet("events.parquet", columns=["name"], filters=where("id", ">", 10)) write_parquet(frame, "selected.parquet", compression="zstd", atomic=true) return 0 Reads eagerly return an independently owned, chunked DataFrame and close the reader. Writes borrow their input and return none only after checked finalization. The full result must fit in memory; batch_size is not a total memory limit. Choose atomic publication explicitly when existing output must survive a failed write; see the safe-write contract for its limits. Option declarations and validation live in irx.analysis.table_io , irx.parquet_options , and packages/arx/src/arx/stdlib/parquet.x . The generated table_io reference supplies Python signatures; the workflow and safety rules below apply to the native engine. Explicit keywords override an options snapshot even when equal to a default . Selections and filters replace, not append to, the corresponding settings. The options owner is never mutated. Unknown parameters, empty selections and unsupported values fail rather than falling back. Without options , reads inspect the path, treating files as files and directories as Hive-aware datasets; suffixes are irrelevant. Writes with partition_columns select Hive dataset mode. Explicit options preserves its existing dataset/Hive policy instead of enabling discovery automatically.

text: Arx Projects and Imports The Arx compiler can read project metadata from .arxproject.toml . The compiler uses this metadata for source layout, import resolution, output defaults, and test discovery. ArxPM provides higher-level project and environment workflows. Project layout A conventional source tree is: . ├── .arxproject.toml ├── src │ └── geometry │ ├── __init__.x │ ├── shared │ │ └── math.x │ └── shapes │ ├── area.x │ └── helpers.x └── tests └── test_area.x Manifest [project] name = "geometry" version = "0.1.0" requires-arx = ">=1.0,<2" dependencies = [ "sciarx>=0.0.3,<1", ] [environment] kind = "conda" name = "geometry" [build-system] dependencies = [ "arxlang>=1.0,<2", ] [build] src_dir = "src" out_dir = "build" package = "geometry" requires-arx uses standard version-specifier syntax. Project dependencies use standard requirement strings and may also be direct references. The compiler validates the manifest but does not install dependencies during import resolution. Use ArxPM or another environment tool to provision them. Imports import geometry.shapes.area import geometry.shapes.area as area import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area import circle_area as area_of_circle from geometry.shapes.area import (circle_area, square_area) from geometry.shapes.area import helper from .helpers import clamp from ..shared.math Relative imports require the from form. Plain import .area is not supported. The resolver checks local project modules before installed Arx packages. The compiler reserves: stdlib for bundled Arx modules, including native-backed Arrow APIs builtins for compiler-injected source modules import math from stdlib fn main() -> i32: return math.square(4) Build settings Libraries may bind native artifacts and system libraries to their own extern modules. See External Native Packages for versioned metadata, package-relative paths, distribution layout, and the C ABI contract. The [build] table can select: src_dir : source root package : default package/module root out_dir : build output directory mode : project build mode when supported by the invoking tool The arx command compiles an entry file and resolves its imported module graph. ArxPM owns workspace-level commands such as project initialization, dependency installation, build, run, packaging, and publishing. Test settings The optional [tests] table controls compiled test discovery: [tests] paths = ["tests", "integration"] exclude = ["tests/experimental_*.x"] file_pattern = "test_*.x" function_pattern = "test_*" See Compiled Tests for the test function contract and CLI flags.

text: Arx Preview Contracts These safety and compatibility decisions describe the non-stable 2026-preview edition (language draft 0.1.0 ). They are not a complete language specification. The capability matrix is the single support summary; executable conformance lives in the compiler tests. Arithmetic and evaluation Boolean evaluation Scalar && / and and || / or require Boolean operands. The left operand is evaluated first. For lhs && rhs , rhs is evaluated only when lhs is true . For lhs || rhs , rhs is evaluated only when lhs is false . packages/arx/tests/arx/test_datatypes.x contains the black-box conformance case: the skipped operand deliberately asserts false. IRx also verifies that lowering uses conditional blocks and a merge value rather than eager LLVM and / or instructions. Boolean negation accepts ! and not . Word not binds below comparisons and above and / or : not a == b means not (a == b) , whereas !a == b means (!a) == b . Parenthesize word negation in tighter operands. Neither spelling adds numeric truthiness. Nullable/Series masks keep their existing eager, null-propagating operations rather than scalar short-circuiting. Prefix increment and decrement Use ++value or --value to update a mutable numeric variable by one. Both expressions yield the updated value: var value: i32 = 3 var increased: i32 = ++value # value and increased are now 4 var decreased: i32 = --value # value and decreased are now 3 Postfix value++ and value-- are not supported. Use prefix mutation or an ordinary assignment such as value = value + 1 or value = value - 1 . Integer mutation follows the checked overflow rules below. Compound assignment += , -= , *= , /= , and %= update a declared mutable numeric variable: var start: i32 = 207 var amount: i32 = 5 start -= amount start %= 100 # start is now 2 Targets must be identifiers, not fields or subscripts. Boolean, string, collection, and nullable operands are unsupported. Compound assignment is a statement, not an expression for arguments, conditions, or returns. It is also allowed in a count-loop update , where it must target that loop's induction variable. The old target value is loaded before evaluating the RHS once, and the result is stored once. Operand promotion and storage must both be lossless: there is no implicit narrowing or wrapping. Integer arithmetic follows the checked rules below, including truncating division and dividend-sign remainder. A failed operation or RHS conversion does not perform the compound store; independent RHS side effects are not rolled back. For example, x += ++x adds the old x to its incremented value, and an overflow in the addition retains that prior increment. Fixed-width integer overflow Fixed-width signed and unsigned 8–64-bit integer + , - , * , negation, and supported increment/decrement operations are checked in every build. IRx fixed-width range induction is checked too; the stdlib range helper uses wider endpoint arithmetic to terminate safely on an overshooting step. Overflow fails before storing or publishing a result; an unused expression is still checked. Provably evaluated invalid constant operations are semantic errors. Untaken branches and short-circuited operands do not execute checks. Implicit numeric conversions preserve the entire source type's domain . Mixed operands use the smallest supported lossless common domain: i32 + u32 computes in i64 , and i32 + f32 in f64 ; i64 + u64 and i64 + f64 require an explicit conversion. A destination annotation never widens a computation retroactively. Same-type templates keep their selected type; widen operands or select math.square<i64>(narrow) before multiplication, not afterward. Source integer literals use the declared/argument/peer type when representable, otherwise default to i32 , then i64 . Uncontextualized floating literals default to f32 . Decimal literals retain their exact value until type selection, then round directly to the chosen binary format, nearest with ties to even. Explicitly typed ASTx literals are never recontextualized. Generic inference uses concrete arguments before contextualizing literal arguments, independently of argument order; literals do not make conflicting concrete same- T arguments compatible. cast(value, Type) checks integer range, including equal-width signedness changes. Float-to-integer casts truncate toward zero, then require a finite, representable result. Explicit integer-to-float and float-narrowing casts may round; finite input must not become infinity. Existing floating NaN, infinity, signed zero, and ordinary IEEE floating arithmetic are preserved. Implicit integer-to-float conversions may not discard integer precision. Intentional modulo arithmetic requires wrapping_add , wrapping_sub , wrapping_mul , or wrapping_cast(value, IntegerType) . Binary wrapping operands must have the same integer type, or an explicit lossless specialization such as wrapping_add<i64>(narrow, 1) . Boolean and floating operands are rejected. These forms do not change surrounding expressions' checked behavior. Integer division and remainder failures Signed integer / truncates toward zero. Scalar % is the remainder from that quotient, so -5 / 100 == 0 and -5 % 100 == -5 , unlike Python's floor-modulo result 95 . % , * , and / have equal precedence and associate left. For a positive integer modulus m , compute r = value % m and add m only when r < 0 ; unlike (r + m) % m , this avoids overflowing on an already positive remainder. The compiled datatype tests exercise this workflow. Integer division and remainder reject zero divisors and signed minimum with negative one before LLVM executes the operation. Remainder supports signed, unsigned, and floating non-nullable scalars, not collections, nullable values, or vectors. Integer SIMD division checks every supplied active lane; no masked source-vector API is implied. Floating-point division follows IEEE behavior; floating % uses truncating remainder (like fmod ), preserves the dividend's sign including negative zero, and produces NaN for a zero divisor. Dynamic integer zero divisors raise ZeroDivisionError ; out-of-range arithmetic and conversions raise OverflowError , at every optimization level. Diagnostic codes remain ARX-RUNTIME-ARITHMETIC-001 and ARX-RUNTIME-CONVERSION-001 . These failures propagate through generated cleanup edges and can be caught; uncaught exceptions produce structured reports and a nonzero exit status. Statically invalid expressions remain compile-time diagnostics. See the exception support boundary . Nullable and Series arithmetic retains checked Arrow kernels, status checking, null propagation, and checked reduction accumulators. Nullable scalar casts skip invalid payloads entirely. Tensor element operations use scalar checks; bulk tensor arithmetic and nonidentity Series/tensor casts are rejected rather than reinterpreting storage. List length/search results must fit their public i32 domain. Numeric runtime unions require lossless shared storage; generic union bounds are membership constraints and need no runtime storage. Raw FFI internals and external native functions remain outside these language guarantees. Ownership The runtime ownership contract owns the detailed create/borrow/move/release rules for lists, strings, files, and class references. Dynamic lists are move-only and cleaned up on ordinary lexical exits, not process-lifetime allocations. Shared class references follow a different model. Use the class lifecycle guide for construction and field ownership, and the file guide for shared cursor and close behavior. IRx cleanup paths for break / continue or generators do not establish Arx source support for those constructs. Fatal errors do not generally unwind caller frames. Do not depend on automatic cleanup to confirm successful writer finalization; follow the CSV or Parquet close contract. Modules and failures Module graph failures One entry module identifies a compiler-owned, canonical dependency graph. Missing modules are IRX-S011 failures and import cycles are IRX-S012 failures; a cycle is never executed or initialized partially. A canonical module is resolved and analyzed once per compilation session. Module-level runtime initialization order remains outside the stable subset until Arx admits and specifies executable module-level statements. Compiled assertions raise AssertionError . Uncaught exceptions emit ARX_EXCEPTION records with stable operation codes and ARX_EXCEPTION_FRAME records for recorded call sites, then exit nonzero. The test runner and ArxPy decode these reports without treating completed subprocess failures as Python compiler errors. Unrecoverable native or exception-machinery allocation failures retain the ARX_RUNTIME_FAIL fallback; they do not promise recovery or cleanup. Compatibility identifiers language draft: 0.1.0 ; source edition: 2026-preview ; compiler diagnostic JSON schema: 1 ; RecordBatch native C ABI: 2 . The language draft and preview edition do not grant source compatibility. Before Arx 2.0, replace APIs within the requested scope and update callers, tests, source contracts, and necessary guides together. Record intentional breaking changes in concise release notes rather than parallel deprecated API documentation. Native ABI producers and consumers must remain aligned. Diagnostics contract Stable compiler failures will have a code, phase, message, and a trustworthy optional source location. Normal CLI use renders expected Arx and IRx failures without a Python traceback and exits nonzero. Unexpected internal failures are not relabeled as user errors. The source loader emits ARX-SOURCE-* , the lexer emits ARX-LEX-* , the parser emits ARX-PARSE-* , and IRx formats its diagnostic families as IRX-* . --diagnostic-format json emits schema version 1 for structured compiler-phase failures. The complete stable-code catalog remains GA work; schema versions must be checked rather than inferred. Decisions still required A stable specification still needs floating-point non-finite/NaN and narrowing rules, broader Unicode operations, general resource/error propagation, FFI and artifact guarantees, and a versioned conformance suite. Do not promote a preview behavior to a compatibility promise without that evidence. At Arx 2.0, explicitly define source/package/native ABI compatibility, edition changes, any deprecation policy, supported toolchains, and release support periods. The pre-2.0 policy must not silently continue afterward.

text: Boolean evaluation Scalar && / and and || / or require Boolean operands. The left operand is evaluated first. For lhs && rhs , rhs is evaluated only when lhs is true . For lhs || rhs , rhs is evaluated only when lhs is false . packages/arx/tests/arx/test_datatypes.x contains the black-box conformance case: the skipped operand deliberately asserts false. IRx also verifies that lowering uses conditional blocks and a merge value rather than eager LLVM and / or instructions. Boolean negation accepts ! and not . Word not binds below comparisons and above and / or : not a == b means not (a == b) , whereas !a == b means (!a) == b . Parenthesize word negation in tighter operands. Neither spelling adds numeric truthiness. Nullable/Series masks keep their existing eager, null-propagating operations rather than scalar short-circuiting.

text: Arx Lexical Syntax The authoritative token spellings, aliases, and editor-tooling inventory live in packages/arx/src/arx/lexer/syntax.json . This guide covers writing source and important restrictions, not a duplicate token catalog. Parser and semantic support is summarized in the capability matrix . Source files and whitespace recognized extensions: .x and .arx indentation is significant the canonical indentation unit is 2 spaces tabs outside quoted literal contents are rejected; use spaces newlines delimit logical lines blank lines do not create indentation transitions Files must be valid UTF-8 and no larger than 4 MiB of UTF-8 bytes. Token start locations use one-based lines and Unicode code-point columns. The lexer also limits delimiter nesting to 256, numeric tokens to 4,096 characters, and non-EOF tokens to 250,000. These are compiler-version resource limits, not a frozen language compatibility promise. fn absolute(value: i32) -> i32: if value < 0: return 0 - value else: return value Comments and docstrings # starts a line comment. Block comments are not supported. Triple backticks delimit Douki YAML docstrings and produce a dedicated docstring token: ``` title: Module documentation summary: Optional description. ``` Docstring placement and schema validation are parser concerns documented in Docstrings . Identifiers Identifiers start with a Unicode letter or _ and continue with Unicode alphanumeric characters or _ . Reference pattern for Unicode-aware tooling: (?:[_\p{L}])(?:[_\p{L}\p{N}])* The exact Unicode categories currently follow the Python runtime. Matching is case-sensitive. Reserved forms Lexical reservation does not promise parsing or lowering. In particular, general const , then , and operator declarations remain unavailable even though their spellings are recognized. Numeric literals Supported forms: decimal integers: 0 , 42 decimal floats with one dot: 3.14 , .5 , 5. Not supported: hexadecimal, binary, or octal prefixes exponent notation such as 1e9 separators such as 1_000 literal suffixes such as 42u32 Multiple dots are invalid, and . by itself is punctuation rather than a number. Strings and characters Double quotes create string literals. Single quotes create character literals. The lexer recognizes these escapes: Escape Value \\ backslash \n newline \r carriage return \t tab \" double quote \' single quote Raw strings, triple-quoted strings, and interpolation are not supported. Triple backticks are reserved for Douki docstrings, not ordinary string values. Structural forms Declaration modifiers @[public, static, constant] version: i32 = 1 Recognized modifiers are public , private , protected , static , constant , mutable , abstract , and extern . Templates @<T: i32 | f64> fn identity(value: T) -> T: return value Explicit template calls use angle brackets: identity<f64>(1.5) . Imports Grouped imports use parentheses, require from , and allow a trailing comma: import ( sin, cos, tan as tangent, ) from math Collection annotations See type annotations . Literal ellipsis has different support boundaries for runtime-shaped tensors and runtime-schema DataFrames; it is not uniformly parameter-only. Consistency rule Changes to lexical syntax update the manifest first, then tokenization, parser, tests, and derived editor consumers. Update this short guide only for changed workflows or restrictions. File , open , and dunder method names remain identifiers, not new keywords. Class lifecycle hooks do not add Arx with statements. Named calls use resolved signatures, not lexical privilege based on the callee's spelling.
